title: Facile Synthesis of Nanostructural High-Performance Cu–Pb Electrocatalysts for CO2 Reduction
abstract: CO2 electroreduction (CO2ER) to chemicals and fuels by renewable electricity is a promising strategy to cope with climate change and fossil fuel depletion crisis.[1–4] In the electrolysis process, hydrogen evolution overwhelms CO2 reduction and therefore highly efficient electrocatalysts are required to regulate the competition between hydrogen evolution and CO2 reduction.[5–7] Development of nonnoble metal catalysts is essential for largescale applications and transition metals are of great potential as catalysts for CO2ER. Of transition metals, Cu and post-transition metals (Pb, Sn, In, Bi) are promising materials, primarily because of Cu’s low cost, high abundance, and catalytic activity and the post-transition metals’ high overpotentials of H2 evolution.[10] Among these four post-transition metals, Pb exhibits high H2 overpotential and excellent selectivity to HCOOH, a key and basic chemical in widespread applications.[11,12] However, pristine polycrystalline Cu catalyst suffers instability and poor selectivity toward reduction products, including carbon monoxide, formic acid, hydrocarbon fuels (e.g., methane), and alcohols (e.g., methanol),[13,14] while low total current density (ranging from −0.6 to −5.5 mA cm−2) at the potential lower than −1.2 V versus reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) and inconsistent faradic efficiency (ranging from 5% to 90%) are the major disadvantages of Pb.[15–20] Previous studies demonstrate that nanostructure, morphology, and crystalline structure are critical to catalytic performance for transition metals electrocatalysts.[8,9] Various methods, including annealing treatment, anodic oxidation, and alkali oxidation–dehydration, have been investigated to prepare nanostructural and monocrystalline Cu.[5] Li et al. modified Cu electrodes by annealing commercial Cu foils in air at 500 °C followed by electrochemical reduction and obtained CO2 reduction geometric current densities >1 mA cm−2 at overpotentials <0.4 V and stable performance over several hours, as compared with <1 h for a polycrystalline Cu electrode.[21] Cu nanowires (NWs) were also prepared by annealing treatment of Cu mesh, achieving a current density of −17 mA cm−2 at −0.9 V versus RHE and low overpotential for CO2 reduction.[22] Annealing treatment has been proved effective and efficient for growing nanostructures on the surface of a variety of transition Nanostructure and crystallinity of transition metals play an important role in catalyzing carbon dioxide electroreduction (CO2ER) where Cu is a typical electrocatalyst with a wide variety of products and Pb has a high overpotential for H2 evolution and is selective toward formic acid. In this study, 3D hierarchical nanostructures of Cu–Pb catalyst are prepared by a two-step electrodepositing–annealing–electroreduction approach (EAE). Cu nanowires (Cu NWs) of 200–400 nm diameter are built on the surface of commercial nickel foam substrates through an EAE step. Then, Pb nanoparticles with diameter of 5–10 nm are uniformly created on the surface of Cu NWs by a second EAE step. The nanostructural Cu–Pb electrodes catalyze CO2ER at a current density of −9.35 mA cm−2 (at −0.93 V vs reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE)). The H2 evolution is suppressed by 35.6% and CO and HCOOH are enhanced by 29.6% and 9.2%, respectively, as compared with Cu NWs. The protocol proposed in this study provides a simple and straightforward approach for preparing high-performance, hierarchical nanostructures of Cu– Pb bimetal catalyst for CO2ER.

1. Introduction
CO2 electroreduction (CO2ER) to chemicals and fuels by renewable electricity is a promising strategy to cope with climate change and fossil fuel depletion crisis.[1–4] In the electrolysis process, hydrogen evolution overwhelms CO2 reduction and therefore highly efficient electrocatalysts are required to regulate the competition between hydrogen evolution and CO2 reduction.[5–7] Development of nonnoble metal catalysts is essential for largescale applications and transition metals are of great potential as catalysts for CO2ER.[8,9] Of transition metals, Cu and post-transition metals (Pb, Sn, In, Bi) are promising materials, primarily because of Cu’s low cost, high abundance, and catalytic activity and the post-transition metals’ high overpotentials of H2 evolution.[10] Among these four post-transition
metals, Pb exhibits high H2 overpotential and excellent selectivity to HCOOH, a key and basic chemical in widespread applications.[11,12] However, pristine polycrystalline Cu catalyst suffers instability and poor selectivity toward reduction products, including carbon monoxide, formic acid, hydrocarbon fuels (e.g., methane), and alcohols (e.g., methanol),[13,14] while low total current density (ranging from −0.6 to −5.5 mA cm−2) at the potential lower than −1.2 V versus reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) and inconsistent faradic efficiency (ranging from 5% to 90%) are the major disadvantages of Pb.[15–20]

metals.[23–25] However, the annealing treatment is not promising for preparing nanostructural Pb, primarily due to its intrinsic agglomeration properties.[26] Nevertheless, Chang and Kanan[15] obtained Pb particles of 100–500 nm by long pulsed anodization followed by electroreduction, achieving a faradaic efficiency (FE) of 97% for HCOOH but a low current density (−0.6 mA cm−2 at −0.8 V vs RHE). More recently, Fan et al.[27] obtained a 3D porous Pb in a surface structure of dendrites 22 × 200 nm by a “Dynamic Hydrogen Bubble Templating” technique, reaching a current density of −7.5 mA cm−2 at −0.99 V versus RHE with an FE of 97% for HCOOH. Fan et al.’s work demonstrates that porous and 3D nanostructural Pb electrocatalysts possess high performance of CO2ER.
Early in 1991, Cu–Pb bimetal electrode was reported to enhance the FE for HCOOH to 50% from 22% and 7% by Cu and Pb electrodes at −1.15 V versus SHE.[20] Recently, nanostructural Cu–Bi,[28] Cu–In,[29,30] and Cu–Sn[31–34] catalysts were obtained by meticulous steps of electrodeposition or chemical deposition for enhanced CO2ER performance with total current densities of 0.6–7.9 mA cm−2 and FEs of 83–93% for electrolysis products CO and HCOOH. In spite of high overpotential for hydrogen evolution on Pb, 3D nanostructural Cu–Pb catalysts have not been reported. This work was aimed to develop an electrodeposition– annealing–electroreduction (EAE) approach for preparing hierarchical nanostructures of Cu–Pb bimetal electrocatalyst by building Pb nanoparticles (NPs) on Cu NWs arrays growing on 3D Ni foam substrates. The prepared Cu–Pb electrodes possess high performance toward CO2ER in terms of current density and controllable selectivity for H2, CO, and HCOOH.

sections.heading: 2. Results and Discussion
sections.text:
Annealing treatment for Cu particles and commercial Cu foils is highly efficient to produce Cu nanostructures.[21,35,36] In this study, nickel foam (NF) was employed as a 3D framework substrate because of its large spe-
cific surface area, exceptional mechanical and thermal strength. Cu was electrochemically deposited on the NF and then annealed in air at 500 °C followed by electrochemical reduction of the resultant Cu oxides. As such, Cu NWs with diameters of 200–400 nm were densely grown on the porous Ni skeleton (Figure 1a,b). The electrodeposition of Pb on the surface of Cu NWs produced clusters of irregularly and unevenly distributed polygonal Pb particles (labeled Pbed/Cu NWs, see Figure 1c,d). Upon annealing at 300 °C in air and electrochemical reduction, the irregular polygonal structures were transformed into NPs of 5–10 nm, which were uniformly distributed on the surface of Cu NWs (labeled Pbar/Cu NWs, see Figure 1e,f). The transmission electron microscope (TEM) characterization (Figure 1g,h) shows that the lattice distance in shell area is 0.310 nm, representing the (111) plane of Pb2O (PDF#75-0201), which was due to the oxidation of lead by air during the manipulation

of the characterization. As a result, a 3D hierarchical nanostructure of Cu–Pb was successfully constructed on the Ni foam substrate. The 3D structures such as Cu mesh[22] and Cu foam[37] of large specific surface areas have been employed as the substrate to prepare highly dense Cu NWs. However, the mechanical and thermal stability of Cu foam is much weaker than Ni foam and we found that Cu foam deformed during the annealing treatment in this work.
The surface composition of Cu NWs, Pbed/Cu NWs, and Pbar/Cu NWs by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) chacterization is shown in Figure 2 and Figure S1 in the Supporting Information. Cu, Ni, and O elements are clearly identified in Cu NWs and Pbed/Cu NWs (Figure 2a and Figure S1a–d, Supporting Information) and Pb is found in Pbed/Cu NWs and Pbar/Cu NWs (Figure 2a,b and Figure S1e, Supporting Information). Interestingly, Ni species are not found in Pbar/Cu NWs (Figure 2a,d) and this is likely that the re-distribution of Pb by the second annealing treatment for Pbed/Cu NWs resulted in a complete coverage of the surface. As for the elemental speciation, both zero-valent metals (Cu, Pb, and Ni) and their oxides are identified and the metal oxides are the results of re-oxidation by air during the storage and characterization.[38] In particular, Pb is prone to oxidation in air to form freshly native oxide (Pb Ntv Ox)[38] and Kumawat and Sarkar[12] have proved that the Pb peak at 138.5 eV was PbO formed during the manipulation of the characterization.
The effect of Pb amount deposited on the morphology and structure of Pbar/Cu NWs was investigated by varying the deposition charge quantity (different electrodeposition time at the same current density; Figure 3). The surface
microstructures of Pbar/Cu NWs were transformed from NPs into nanosheets (or platelet-like) with increasing the deposition charge from 15 to 150 C. The X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis shows that the intensities of NiO (PDF#78-0643), Ni (PDF#870712), and Cu (PDF#85-1326) peaks decreased and the intensity of Pb (PDF#87-0663) increased with increasing the deposition charge. Energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS) results show that the mole concentration of Pb relative to the sum of Cu and Pb increased from 5.06% to 43.99%. The platelet-like structures of Pb were also observed on inert glassy carbon or nickel electrodes by electroplating in alkaline ionic liquids.[39]
Cyclic voltammetry (CV) was tested on Pbar/Cu NWs, Cu NWs, and Pb foil in the solution of 0.5 m KOH purged with argon (Figure S2, Supporting Information). The oxidation peaks of Cu [Cu→Cu(I)→Cu(II)] and the reduction peak of PbO [PbO→Pb] on Pbar/Cu NWs confirm the presence of Cu and Pb elements on the surface. The reduction peak of PbO to Pb has been previously observed on Pb/C electrode (around 0.1 V vs RHE)[12] and Pb foil electrode (around 0 V vs RHE)[40] in similar electrolyte systems. Clearly, the current density of Pbar/Cu NWs was much lower than that of Cu NWs, indicating that Pb significantly suppressed the H2 evolution reaction (HER). Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) tests for Pbar/Cu NWs in Ar and CO2 purging 0.5 m KHCO3 solutions are shown in Figure S3 in the Supporting Information. The current density obtained in CO2 purging KHCO3 solutions for the potentials over −0.4 V versus RHE was substantially higher than that obtained in Ar purging KHCO3 solutions. This demonstrates that Pbar/Cu NWs is effective to catalyze CO2 reduction. The performance of three typical catalysts (Cu NWs, Pbed/Cu NWs, and Pbar/Cu NWs) for

CO2ER is shown in Figure 4. The FE of the main electrolysis products H2, CO, and HCOOH by Cu NWs was 54.8%, 31.0%, and 12.7%, respectively, at −0.93 V versus RHE in CO2-purging 0.5 m KHCO3 (by contrast, H2 FE on the bare Ni foam was 99.8% under the same electrolysis condition). Electrodepositing Pb with passing charge of 30 C on Cu NWs suppressed H2 production by 11.0% and enhanced HCOOH by 12.4% while transforming deposited Pb into NPs further suppressed H2 production by 19.6% and enhanced CO by 16.2%. Nevertheless, Pb decoration of Cu NWs decreased the total current density of CO2ER (−10.8 mA cm−2 at −0.93 V vs RHE) by 22.2% on Pbed/Cu NWs and 13.0% on Pbar/Cu NWs. Clearly, the suppression of H2 evolution and enhancement of CO and HCOOH efficiencies were related to Ni annihilation and Pb decoration on the surface of the catalysts (see previous discussion related to Figures 1–3). In particular, the thin layer of Pb oxides NPs was primarily responsible. Chang and Kanan observed that the Pb oxide layer of Pb foil electrode passivated the surface for H2 evolution and activated for CO2 reduction.[15] It should be noted

that the FE (selectivity) of CO2ER by Pb-doped Cu obtained in this study was less profound than Sn-doped Cu reported in the literatures,[31–34] despite that hydrogen evolution overpotential of Pb is higher than that of Sn. This is partially because Cu and Sn have solid solutions or intermetallics, which have synergistic effect on catalytic reduction of CO2. Nevertheless, EAE is a straightforward approach for modifying the surface morphology, textural, and composition of a core metal substrate for enhanced performance of CO2ER.
The C2+ compounds obtained by Cu–Pb NWs in this study included acetate, ethanol, and propyl alcohol. A wide variety of C2+ compounds have been observed by nanostructure Cu-based electrocatalysts.[41,42] Despite that the mechanism for CO2ER has not been well understood, it is well accepted that the process is a series of electrochemical-induced hydrogenation reactions, in which the adsorption of intermediate products on the catalyst is critical to the performance of CO2ER.[5,7] CO is the first intermediate product of CO2 reduction catalyzed by Cu and further converted to higher-valued products using H2O as a living hydrogen source.[43,44] Extensive studies have demonstrated that bimetals and alloys promote CO2ER performance, probably due to the metal-to-metal interactions and the interface effects between different active materials.[45] The hydrogen overflow effect,[46] a characteristic advantage of bimetal electrocatalysts, that suppresses HER and facilitates CO2 hydrogenation.[47] The particle size and distribution of the deposited metal and the type of metal substrates are important to determine such effects.[48]
The CO2ER performance of the Pbar/Cu NWs catalysts with different Pb deposition charges is shown in Figure 5. H2 evolution decreased with increasing the amount of Pb loaded and reached a minimum at the deposition charge of 30 C, at which the best performance of CO2ER was achieved (Figure 5a). The CO2ER performance did not change significantly between the deposition charge of 15 and 45 C whereas a further increase of deposition charge from 45 to 75 C resulted in a drastic drop in the efficiency of CO2 reduction. A complete loss of CO production was observed and the electrolysis product was solely HCOOH for the deposition charge of 150 C, which was actually the characteristic of Pb. The total current density of the electrolysis decreased monotonically with increasing the passing charge and the partial current densities of CO and HCOOH reached a maximum value while the partial current density of
H2 was on a valley at the passing charge of 30 C (Figure 5b). Similar trends were also observed for other Cu-based electrodes including Cu–Ag[49] and Cu–Sn[32,34] bimetal electrocatalysts.
Effect of applied potential on the CO2ER performance of Cu NWs and Pbar/Cu NWs catalysts is displayed in Figure S4 in the Supporting Information. Apparently, the CO2ER efficiencies increase with increasing applied potential and the best performance of Pbar/Cu NWs was achieved at −0.93 V (vs RHE) with an FE of 49.51%, 23.21%, and 4.86% for CO, HCOOH, and C2+ compounds, respectively. By contrast, the best performance of Cu NWs was achieved at −0.93 V (vs RHE) with FE of 37.04% and 13.78% for CO and HCOOH, respectively. The partial current densities of Cu NWs and Pbar/Cu NWs for CO, HCOOH, and H2 in the potentials between −0.23 and −1.13 V versus RHE are shown in Figure 6. There was a significant difference in the partial current density of H2 between these two catalysts in the tested potential range whereas the partial current densities for HCOOH and CO were not profound. The stability of Pbar/Cu NWs catalyst was conducted at −0.93 V versus RHE and the total current density and the FE were relatively constant during the testing period of 20 000 s (Figure 7).

Finally, it was noted that CO/H2 ratios of 2.3–2.7 were obtained in the best performance of CO2ER in this work. These ratios are well within the CO/H2 ratio of syngas for industrial Fischer–Tropsch synthesis.[50,51] A gas-phase product of syngas’ composition and a highly selective liquid-phase product of HCOOH by CO2ER would be of advantages when the total current density, FE, and energy efficiency are taken into account, because CO2 conversion by electrochemical route to long-chain hydrocarbons and oxygenates is much more difficult than to CO and HCOOH in terms of the thermodynamic and kinetics.

sections.heading: 3. Conclusions
sections.text: 3D hierarchical nanostructures of Cu–Pb electrocatalysts for high-performance CO2 reduction have been susscesfully prepared by EAE on NFs. Cu was electrodeposited onto Ni foams in 0.5 m CuSO4 and 1.0 m H2SO4 solutions and subsequent annealing treatment at 500 °C followed by electroreduction in 0.5 m KHCO3 solution produced Cu NWs of 200–400 nm diameter. Pb clusters were then electrodeposited onto the Cu NWs and uniformly re-distributed in particle sizes of 5–10 nm by annealing treatment. The preparation procedure is simple and straightforward in producing hierarchical nanostructures of Cu–Pb bimetal catalysts. FEs of 19.2%, 50.6%, and 22.0% for H2, CO, and HCOOH with a total current density of −9.35 mA cm−2 at −0.93 V versus RHE were obtained by the Cu–Pb catalyst with Pb decoration of 30 C. The CO/H2 ratios were in the range of typical syngas for industrial Fischer– Tropsch synthesis. The use of Ni foams as porous 3D substrates through electrodeposition and annealing treatment is of great potential to tune the catalytic activity of bimetal catalysts for efficient electroreduction of CO2.

sections.heading: 4. Experimental Section
sections.text:
Chemicals: NF of 1.5 mm thickness (99.8% purity, 380 g m−2 surface density),Cu foil of 0.6 mm thickness (99.999%), and Pb foil of 0.6 mm
thickness (99.99%) were purchased from Qinghe Jinjia Metal Materials Co, Ltd, China. Saturated calomel electrode (SCE) was purchased from CH Instruments Inc, US. CuSO4·5H2O (99.7%), H2SO4 (95%∼98%), NaOH (99.7%), CH3COONa·3H2O (99.7%), NaKC4H4O6·4H2O (99.7%), Pb(CH2COO)2·3H2O (99.7%), and HCl (36.5%∼38%) were obtained from Beijing Chemical Works, China. KHCO3 (99.97%) was obtained from Aladdin Industrial Co., US. Analytical grade chemicals, deionized water, and gaseous CO2 (>99.99%) were used in this study.
Electrode Preparation: In the synthesis strategy, several simple steps of electroreduction and thermal treatment were employed: growing Cu on NF and attaching Pb on Cu by electrodepositing and annealing treatment to construct typical microstructure.
First, pristine NF (3 cm × 3 cm) was washed with ethanol and 0.5 m HCl for 15 min each to remove attached organic compound and native oxide layer. After rising with deionized water, the prepared NF was thorough dried. For Cu electrodeposition on NF, constant current (−1.5 A) was applied with prepared NF as cathode immersed into a solution of 0.5 m CuSO4 and 1.0 m H2SO4 for 2000 s. The fresh sample was washed several times with deionized water and thorough dried by blowing Ar gas. The prepared sample was heated at 500 °C for 12 h in air atmosphere and cooled down to room temperature (25–30 °C) over several hours. The annealed dark gray sample was then electrochemically reduced to dark red oxide-derived Cu catalyst in 0.5 m KHCO3 solution at constant potential of −1.8 V versus SCE for several minutes until the reduction current curve became stable.
Then, Pb was electrodeposited on oxide-derived Cu in a twoelectrode system with prepared polished Pb foil as anode, where the electrolyte was an alkaline electroplating solution consisting of 73.23 g L−2 Pb(CH2COO)2·3H2O with 200.08 g L−1 NaOH, 23.4 g L−1 CH3COONa·3H2O, and 26.23 g L−1 NaKC4H4O6·4H2O. Constant current (−1.5 A) was applied with prepared oxide-derived Cu immersed into the alkaline plating solution at 70 °C while varying the deposition charge (15, 30, 60, 75, 150 C). The sample obtained was marked as Pbed/Cu. Followed by drying with blowing Ar gas after washing several times with deionized water, the prepared sample was heated at 300 °C in muffle furnace and cooled down to room temperature over several hours. The annealed sample was then electroreduced in same way. The sample obtained was marked as Pbar/Cu. All the above electrochemical experiments were conducted at room temperature unless stated otherwise.
Characterization: Scanning electron microscope (SEM) images were obtain from a JEOL 6701F microscope equipped with an EDS (ixef). TEM images were obtained at 100.0 kV from a HITACHI HT7700 microscope. XRD patterns were obtained by LabX XRD-6000 with Cu X-ray tube with scan rate of 5° min−1 in the 2θ range of 5–90 °. XPS was measured on Thermo Scientific ESCALAB 250Xi with X-ray excitation provided by Al K α radiation. All the spectra were calibrated by C 1s¼ 284.6 eV.
Electrochemical Measurement: An electrochemical workstation (CHI660E CH Instruments Inc.) was used for all electrochemical measurements including electrodeposition, electrochemical testing, and CO2 electrolysis and the applied potential was corrected by automatic iR compensation function. A two-compartment electrolytic cell was employed throughout the CO2 electrolysis and some electrochemical testing experiments. SELEMIONTM ion exchange membrane (AGC Engineering Co. Ltd., Japan) was used in separating different pole compartments. Each compartment was filled with 20 mL 0.5 m KHCO3 saturated with CO2 (pH = 7.2) as electrolyte, and CO2 was constantly bubbled into the cathodic compartment the volumetric flow of 30 mL min−1 during the electrolysis. Prepared electrodes and RuO2/Ti mesh are employed as working electrode and counter electrode (with an external SCE reference electrode), respectively. Potentials in experiments are reported with respect to the RHE by the following equation: E (RHE) = E (SCE) + 0.242 + 0.0591*pH. CV and LSV experiments were performed in three-electrode system, with prepared catalysts, Pt, SCE used as working electrode, counter electrode and reference electrode, respectively.
A micro gas chromatograph (Agilent Technologies 490, US) was equipped with a 5 Å MolSieve column and Ar as carrier gas. A flame ionization detector and a thermal conductivity detector were used
